title: Prompting, Model Behavior & Structured Outputs
scopeHtml: Scope: tokens, context window, sampling, model tiers, prompting modes, the four prompt techniques, structured outputs and extended thinking. Exam-style scenario multiple choice; the correct option and the reason each wrong option fails are in the answer.

notes.title: Tokens and the context window
notes.html:
Tokens. Claude does not read letters or words; it reads tokens, chunks of text produced by a tokenizer. Everything the model processes and produces is counted in tokens: the system prompt, the whole conversation, tool definitions, tool results, documents, images (converted to tokens), and the response. Tokens are the unit of price, of rate limits and of space in the context window. Characters-per-token averages depend on the model's tokenizer and differ between model generations, so treat any rule of thumb (like "about four characters per token in English") as an estimate and measure with the real counter when it matters.

The context window. A fixed budget: the total number of tokens the model can take in for one request, with input and output sharing it. Two distinct edge behaviours, which exam questions love to confuse:

  1. Input already larger than the window → the request is rejected with a validation error before generation begins.
  2. Input fits, but generation reaches the ceiling → current models stop and return the output generated so far with the stop reason model_context_window_exceeded, rather than raising an error.

In neither case does the API silently drop your oldest messages or summarize for you. If you want a long session to keep running, your application must trim or summarize history before each call (or use the platform's server-side compaction, a beta strategy).

Why development hides the problem. Test inputs are short, so the window rarely fills. Production has longer inputs, more turns, bigger tool results (often three to five times longer than fixtures). A session that handles twenty turns in development can fill the window by turn eight in production. That failure shows up as odd tool selection or incomplete answers, not as a clean error, because early instructions get crowded out.

Budgeting method.

  1. Reserve output tokens first (max_tokens).
  2. Count the fixed parts: system prompt + tool definitions.
  3. Add the current user message and any documents.
  4. Spend what remains on history and retrieved context, trimming by priority.
  5. Verify with count_tokens (same body as a messages call, no inference run) on real production-sized inputs, not test fixtures.

Real life. A restaurant order slip that only fits 40 lines. Starters, mains, special requests and the waiter's notes all share the slip. You cannot write line 41; someone must rewrite the slip shorter, and if the notes are too long, the main course instructions get squeezed out.

Tech. A phone's RAM: apps (history) all share it. Test on a toy phone with three apps and everything is smooth; the user's real phone has forty apps and things start dying.

Exam traps.

  • Counting only words or only the user's text when estimating cost.
  • Believing the API truncates old turns for you.
  • Mixing up "rejected before generation" with "stopped mid-generation".

notes.title: Sampling and non-determinism
notes.html:
Why outputs vary. At every step the model produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens and then samples from it. Settings such as temperature reshape that distribution: lower temperature concentrates probability on the most likely tokens (more repeatable); higher temperature spreads it out (more varied). Because the choice is sampled, the same prompt run twice can return different wording even when both answers are correct.

Important qualifications.

  • Temperature 0 does not guarantee identical output across calls. It makes outputs more repeatable, nothing more.
  • Sampling controls are model-dependent. The newest Claude models do not accept non-default sampling parameters: setting temperature, top_p or top_k returns a 400 error, and behaviour on those models is steered through prompting. Always confirm current parameter support in the API reference at build time.

What it means for testing. A test that asserts the exact text of a response will be flaky because the model can express the same correct answer many ways. Instead:

  • Assert the property that must hold: a required field is present, a value is in range, the output parses against a schema, a label is one of the allowed set.
  • When meaning matters, use an eval with a graded judge (see the evals notes).
  • Run enough samples to measure rates, not single outcomes.

Real life. Asking a friend "what do you want for dinner?" on three different days. The answer may be "pizza", "pasta" or "Italian"; all are valid, and you would not write a rule that requires one exact word.

Tech. A load balancer choosing among healthy servers: which server answers varies, but the property you assert is "a healthy server answered".

Common mistakes.

  • Setting temperature on a model that rejects it, then being surprised by 400s.
  • "Fixing" flaky tests by retrying until they pass.
  • Treating temperature 0 as a determinism switch.

notes.title: Model tiers and reasoning
notes.html:
The family. Claude spans four tiers with different cost, latency and capability trade-offs:

Tier Role
Fable most capable; the hardest reasoning, coding and agentic work where maximum intelligence is the priority
Opus demanding work above the Sonnet envelope
Sonnet the balanced default for most production workloads
Haiku speed and cost efficiency on tasks that fit its capability envelope

Confirm the current lineup and model identifiers against the platform docs at build time; the family evolves.

The default discipline. Start with Sonnet. Move up a tier only when an eval shows the current tier missing your quality bar. Move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable for the task, not merely to save money. A model change is a measured decision.

Reasoning is a separate dial. Which model runs is one decision; whether it reasons before answering is a second, per-request decision. On current models reasoning is adaptive thinking: the model decides how much to think and you tune depth with an effort setting instead of a fixed token budget. The older budget_tokens control is deprecated and, on the newest generations, returns a 400. Thinking content is omitted from responses by default on the newest models; request a summarized display if you need to show it. Per-model defaults differ (some think by default), so confirm them.

How the two levers combine.

  • Capable model, reasoning off: fast and direct.
  • Smaller model, reasoning on: spends more tokens to think.
  • Hardest tasks: a capable model with a higher effort setting.

When reasoning pays. Hard multi-step problems (derivations, constraint problems, planning dependent actions). It is wasted on lookups, classification, extraction and format conversion, where a well-constrained prompt is cheaper and just as accurate. Thinking tokens bill like output tokens.

Real life. Choosing a vehicle (bike, car, truck) is a separate choice from whether to plan your route first. Planning a 200 m walk to the shop is wasted effort; planning a cross-country trip is not.

Tech. Instance size vs "enable debug tracing": independent settings, and you pay for both.

notes.title: Fixing prompts: the four techniques
notes.html:
The principle. A prompt that works in interactive use often breaks in production on untested inputs. The fix is not "more words", it is identifying which structural piece is missing and adding that one piece. Diagnose how the output fails, then apply the matching technique.

What you observe What is missing Why the technique fixes it
Right content, wrong shape (a sentence where you expected a label; prose where you expected JSON) Output constraint Controls the form independent of content; without it you get plausible text your parser was not built for
Scope or tone drifts, worse deeper into the conversation System prompt (or a more specific one) A persistent behavioural contract holding role, scope and format steady across turns
Task understood, but structure invented Few-shot examples One correct input→output pair shows the exact pattern, which a description often cannot pin down
Clean on tested inputs, breaks on a variant A constraint or example covering the variant The prompt handled the happy path only; name the edge case or show one

The four techniques in detail.

  • System prompts carry the behavioural contract for the session: role, rules that must not change, output format.
  • XML tags separate instructions from data (<my_code>, <docs>, <ticket>, <sample_input>, <ideal_output>); use descriptive names that match the content, not "official" ones.
  • Few-shot examples show rather than tell; wrap them in consistent tags so the model does not read them as part of the task. Pull them from your highest-scoring eval outputs.
  • Output constraints are the last line of defence before your parser: specify field names, types, length limits, whether to include preamble, and what to do when data is absent. Use structured outputs when machine-readability is mandatory.

Prompting modes. Zero-shot (instruction only), one-shot (one example), multi-shot/few-shot (several). Examples sit in the prompt; they are not training data. Each costs tokens on every call, so add the fewest that work. A more capable model may succeed zero-shot where a smaller one needs examples, so choose model and example count together against an eval.

The worked failure. A ticket classifier returned "Billing", "billing", and "This looks like a billing issue". Six revision passes each added more words (descriptions, "be concise", edge-case paragraphs); the output stayed broken, and the verbose prompt induced verbose output and latency. The fix was two things: an output constraint ("exactly one of BILLING, TECHNICAL, ESCALATION; return only the label") and two few-shot examples in tags. The lesson: description is not constraint.

Decision rules. Stack all four against a well-defined output contract. Simplify when you over-engineered a trivial task ("summarize this paragraph" needs no schema). If three re-prompts in a row have not worked, stop and diagnose.

Real life. Telling a new barista "make it nice" fails. Handing them a photo of the finished latte (few-shot) and a rule ("8 oz, no extra foam", an output constraint) works.

Tech. An API contract: a vague contract ("return the user") breaks clients; a schema plus an example response does not.

notes.title: Structured outputs
notes.html:
What it is. Instead of asking for a shape in words, you give the API a JSON schema and generation is constrained (constrained decoding): as each token is generated only tokens that keep the output valid against the schema are allowed, so a violating response cannot be produced.

Two flavours.

  • JSON outputs (output_config.format with type: json_schema) constrain the final response. Use when the model itself produces the structured payload your code consumes (field extraction, API-shaped replies). Removes parse-and-retry code.
  • Strict tool use (strict: true on a tool definition) constrains the arguments Claude passes to tools; they are validated against the input schema before your code runs. Use in agentic loops where a malformed argument would crash a function or trigger a wrong action. They can be used together.

Why not just prompt for JSON. A prompt instruction holds on the cases you tried and slips on one you did not; a schema constraint is enforced on every token. It moves correctness from "verify after the fact" to "ruled out before it happens".

Costs and limits to know.

  1. First request on a new schema is slower: the API compiles the schema into a grammar. Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, so stable schemas pay once; constantly changing schemas pay repeatedly.
  2. Input tokens rise: the API injects a format-describing system prompt and bills it.
  3. A guaranteed schema is not a guaranteed success. A refusal (stop_reason: refusal) and a truncation at max_tokens (stop_reason: max_tokens, stopping mid-structure) can still return output that does not match. Always check stop_reason.
  4. Incompatible with message prefilling. Pick one.
  5. It guarantees shape, not truth: a value can be well-formed and wrong.

Real life. A paper form with boxes versus a blank page. People can leave a box empty or decline to fill the form, but they cannot write outside the boxes.

Tech. Typed deserialization versus regex-scraping logs.

notes.title: Extended thinking
notes.html:
What it does. With extended thinking on, the model writes its step-by-step reasoning first, returned as its own thinking block placed just before the block holding the answer, and then gives the final answer. On the newest models the thinking text is omitted by default; request a summarized display to read it. It is enabled through the thinking parameter where not already on by default, and depth is tuned with the effort setting (not budget_tokens, which is deprecated and 400s on the newest generations).

Cost. Thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens, so high effort on a simple task is paying for accuracy you do not need. Match the tool to the task.

When to use it.

Task shape Thinking? Why
Multi-step reasoning holding several constraints (maths derivation, multi-hop logic, planning dependent actions) Enable, effort matched to depth The reasoning pass works through dependencies otherwise skipped
Mechanical/lookup tasks (classification, format conversion, extracting a field, short facts) Off No accuracy gain; a constrained prompt is the right tool
Agentic loops planning across several tool calls Enable, budget for the planning step Reasoning before a plan reduces wrong-tool selection later

The carry-back rule (critical in tool loops). When extended thinking is on and the conversation uses tools, every thinking block you receive must be returned to the API exactly as it arrived on the next turn. Each block carries a signature confirming the reasoning was not tampered with. Edit it, summarize it or drop it and the signature no longer matches, so the API rejects the request. Redacted thinking blocks (encrypted, not human-readable) follow the same rule. It is a structural requirement, not a prompting choice. The classic slip: stripping thinking blocks to save context, which breaks the next request. If accumulated reasoning worries you for context size, solve it with context engineering (compaction, pruning, subagents), never by editing blocks.

Real life. A signed lab report. If you retype or shorten it, the signature no longer matches and the hospital rejects it.

Tech. A JWT: change one byte of the payload and signature verification fails.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Tokens and window. Everything is tokens (price, limits, space). Input + output share the window. Over-large input is rejected before generation; hitting the ceiling mid-generation returns partial output with model_context_window_exceeded. Nothing is silently trimmed; your app trims or summarizes. Production sizes differ from fixtures; measure with count_tokens.

Sampling. Output is sampled, so wording varies. temperature 0 is more repeatable, not deterministic. The newest models reject non-default temperature/top_p/top_k with a 400. Test properties (fields present, parses, in range), not exact strings; use evals for meaning.

Tiers and reasoning. Fable, Opus, Sonnet (default), Haiku. Move up/down only on eval evidence. Model choice and reasoning are independent dials; adaptive thinking is tuned by effort (budget_tokens deprecated). Use reasoning for hard multi-step work, not lookups.

Prompt fixes. Diagnose, then add the missing piece: wrong shape → output constraint; drift → system prompt; invented structure → few-shot; variant failures → constraint/example for the variant. XML tags separate data from instructions. Fewest examples that work. Three failed re-prompts → stop and diagnose. Description is not constraint.

Structured outputs. Schema-constrained generation: JSON outputs for final responses, strict tool use for tool args. Costs: first-call grammar compile (cached 24 h), extra input tokens. Still check stop_reason (refusal, max_tokens). No prefilling. Shape, not truth.

Extended thinking. For multi-step and planning tasks; off for lookups. Thinking tokens bill as output. Return thinking and redacted thinking blocks unchanged in tool loops (signature); manage context by other means.

One-liners.

  • "Fix the structure, not the wording."
  • "A schema is enforcement; a prompt is a request."
  • "Thinking blocks go back untouched."
  • "Window overflow is rejected up front; ceiling-hit stops mid-way."

questions.promptHtml:
A request's input is 30% larger than the model's context window. What happens?

  • A. The oldest messages are silently dropped and the request succeeds
  • B. The request is rejected with a validation error before generation begins
  • C. Claude generates a partial answer with stop reason model_context_window_exceeded
  • D. The API automatically compacts the conversation

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Input that is already larger than the window is rejected before generation. C describes a different case: input fits, but generation hits the ceiling.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: There are two edge behaviors. Input too large: validation error, nothing generated. Input fits but output reaches the ceiling: current models return what was generated with model_context_window_exceeded. Nothing is silently truncated (A) and nothing is compacted for you (D) unless you configure server-side compaction (beta). Trimming or summarizing history before each call is your application's job.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Choosing A because other chat products drop old turns. The API does not.
  • Confusing the input-too-large error with the mid-generation stop reason.

questions.promptHtml:
Your test asserts response.text == "Your refund is approved." and fails intermittently even though every answer is correct. What is the right fix?

  • A. Set temperature to 0 so the output is identical every time
  • B. Assert on the property that must hold (required field present, value in range, structure parses) and use a model-graded eval for meaning
  • C. Retry the test until it passes
  • D. Switch to a larger model

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Sampling makes wording vary; test properties, not exact strings.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The model samples from a probability distribution, so identical inputs do not guarantee identical outputs. Temperature 0 makes output more repeatable but does not guarantee identical output across calls (A). On the newest models, non-default temperature/top_p/top_k return a 400 error anyway. Retrying hides the flake (C) and a bigger model is still non-deterministic (D).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing temperature=0 equals determinism.
  • Sending sampling parameters to the newest models and getting a 400.

questions.promptHtml:
A team runs a cheap lookup-and-classify workload on Sonnet. A colleague proposes "turn on maximum reasoning and move to the top tier for safety." What is the best response?

  • A. Agree; more reasoning always improves accuracy
  • B. Model choice and reasoning are independent levers; keep Sonnet, leave reasoning off for lookups and classification, and only change either after an eval shows a miss
  • C. Reasoning can only be enabled on the top tier, so you must upgrade
  • D. Move to Haiku and enable reasoning to compensate for it

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Start with Sonnet, move only on eval evidence, and spend thinking tokens only on hard multi-step problems.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Which model runs and whether it reasons are separate per-request decisions. Thinking tokens bill like output tokens, so reasoning on a lookup is paid-for accuracy you do not need. The default discipline: Sonnet first, up a tier only when an eval misses the bar, down to Haiku only when an eval says the drop is acceptable. Reasoning is configured with the effort setting on current models; budget_tokens is deprecated and returns 400 on the newest generations.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating "smarter model" and "reasons longer" as the same knob.
  • Choosing a tier by gut feel instead of an eval.

questions.promptHtml:
A support classifier returns "Billing", "billing", and sometimes "This looks like a billing issue." The downstream router breaks. The developer has rewritten the prompt five times, each longer than the last. What is missing?

  • A. A bigger model
  • B. More descriptive paragraphs about each category
  • C. An output constraint (exactly one label from a fixed set, no other text) plus few-shot examples showing the exact casing, wrapped in XML tags
  • D. Extended thinking

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. The content is right and the shape is wrong, which is an output-constraint problem.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Map the symptom to the missing technique: wrong shape → output constraint; scope drift → system prompt; invented structure → few-shot; fails on a variant → a constraint or example covering it. More description (B) does not constrain the form, and long prompts also induce long outputs and latency. After three re-prompts in a row without progress, stop adding text and diagnose. Thinking (D) is wasted on classification.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
System: You are a support classifier. Classify each ticket into exactly one of:
BILLING, TECHNICAL, ESCALATION. Return only the label. No other text.

<sample_input>My account shows two charges for April.</sample_input>
<ideal_output>BILLING</ideal_output>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding more words instead of identifying which technique is absent.
  • Describing the categories at length when the model already understands them.

questions.promptHtml:
You enable JSON-schema structured outputs and assume every response will now parse. Which statement is correct?

  • A. Correct: the schema is enforced on every token, so every response always parses
  • B. A refusal (stop_reason: refusal) or truncation at max_tokens can still return output that does not match the schema, so code must check stop_reason
  • C. Structured outputs can be combined with message prefilling to force the start of the JSON
  • D. The first request on a new schema is faster because it is cached

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. A guaranteed schema is not a guaranteed success.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Structured outputs use constrained decoding (output_config.format with type: json_schema; strict: true for tool arguments). But a refusal or a max_tokens cut-off stops mid-structure. Also: it is incompatible with prefilling (C), the first request on a new schema is slower because the grammar is compiled (cached for 24 hours from last use) (D), and the injected format prompt adds input tokens.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping the stop_reason check.
  • Changing the schema on every request and paying the compile cost repeatedly.

questions.promptHtml:
With extended thinking enabled, an agent loop strips the thinking blocks from history to save context. The next request fails. Why, and what is the correct approach?

  • A. Thinking blocks are too large; the API rejects any request over 10k tokens
  • B. Each thinking block carries a signature; editing, summarizing or dropping it invalidates the request, so return every thinking (and redacted thinking) block unchanged and manage context with other strategies
  • C. The thinking block must be converted to a text block
  • D. Thinking blocks must be re-generated by sending an empty tool_result

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. This is the carry-back rule: thinking blocks go back to the API exactly as received.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: The signature confirms the reasoning was not tampered with. Redacted thinking blocks are encrypted but follow the same rule. If accumulated reasoning worries you, fix it with context engineering (compaction, pruning, subagents), not by editing blocks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the text block next to a tool_use also need preserving? → Yes, keep the full content array.
  2. Should a classifier use extended thinking? → No, a constrained prompt is cheaper and as accurate.

questions.promptHtml:
You are estimating the cost of a feature that sends a system prompt, 12 chat turns, three tool definitions and one tool result per turn. What is the right unit to count?

  • A. Words in the user's messages only
  • B. Characters in the final answer
  • C. Tokens across prompt, history, tool definitions, tool results and the response
  • D. Number of API calls

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. Everything the model processes and produces is billed and budgeted in tokens.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Counting only the user's words (A) or the answer (B) ignores most of the spend; tool definitions and results ride along on every turn. Number of calls (D) says nothing about size. Use count_tokens on a real request to measure.

questions.promptHtml:
A long generation stops early and returns text with stop_reason: model_context_window_exceeded instead of an error. What does this mean?

  • A. The input was too large and was rejected
  • B. The input fit, but generation reached the window ceiling, so you got the output so far
  • C. The model refused for safety reasons
  • D. A rate limit was hit

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Input larger than the window is rejected up front; hitting the ceiling mid-generation returns the partial output with this stop reason.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Do not treat the partial text as complete. Trim or summarize history before the next call. A refusal (C) uses stop_reason: refusal; a rate limit (D) is a 429.

questions.promptHtml:
A team ports a prompt to the newest Claude model and starts getting 400 errors. The request sets temperature: 0.2 and top_p: 0.9. Likely cause?

  • A. Temperature must be 0
  • B. The newest models do not accept non-default sampling parameters; remove them and steer with the prompt
  • C. The API key lacks permission
  • D. The prompt is too long

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Setting temperature, top_p or top_k returns a 400 on the newest models.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Behavior is steered through prompting there. Always confirm current parameter support in the API reference at build time. Even where temperature is accepted, 0 does not guarantee identical output.

questions.promptHtml:
Which test best fits a feature whose answers are correct but worded differently each run?

  • A. assert text == expected
  • B. Assert required fields exist and values are in range; use a model-graded eval for meaning
  • C. Run it 10 times and take the first result
  • D. Set temperature to 0 and keep the string assertion

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Test the property that must hold, not the exact wording.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: String equality fails valid paraphrases. Temperature 0 (D) reduces variance but does not guarantee identity. Picking the first of ten runs (C) tests nothing.

questions.promptHtml:
A task needs a very specific output casing and one tricky edge case that a written description keeps missing. What is the cheapest fix?

  • A. A bigger model
  • B. Add one or two correct input/output examples (few-shot)
  • C. A three-page instruction block
  • D. Lower the temperature

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Examples show the exact shape; one or two usually beat another paragraph.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Examples are in the prompt, not training data, and cost tokens on every call, so add the fewest that work. A more capable model may succeed zero-shot, so choose model and example count together against an eval.

questions.promptHtml:
Claude answers a much wider question than you asked, and the drift gets worse deeper into the conversation. Which piece is missing?

  • A. An output constraint
  • B. A (more specific) system prompt
  • C. A larger context window
  • D. A JSON schema

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Scope and tone drifting across turns means the behavioral contract is too vague.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Wrong shape points to an output constraint (A); invented structure points to few-shot; failure only on variants points to a constraint or example for that variant. Window size (C) is unrelated.

questions.promptHtml:
A prompt asks Claude to debug code using pasted documentation, and Claude blurs the two. What helps most?

  • A. Capitalize the instructions
  • B. Wrap them in descriptive tags such as <my_code> and <docs>
  • C. Repeat the instruction three times
  • D. Put the docs after the code with no markers

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Descriptive XML tags make the boundary between inputs and instructions unambiguous.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: You need not use official tag names; names that match the content work best. Use consistent tags for examples (<sample_input>, <ideal_output>) so the model does not read them as part of the task.

questions.promptHtml:
Why is a JSON schema constraint more reliable than the instruction "return only JSON"?

  • A. The model reads schemas more carefully
  • B. The API enforces it at generation time, token by token, so edge cases you never tested cannot slip
  • C. It makes the model faster on every call
  • D. It removes the need for any error handling

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. A prompt instruction is a request; a schema is enforcement.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: It is not free: a first-call grammar compile, extra input tokens, and refusal or max_tokens can still produce non-matching output. Error handling stays (D is wrong).

questions.promptHtml:
Which setting guarantees that tool arguments are validated against the input schema before your code runs?

  • A. strict: true on the tool definition
  • B. required on every field
  • C. Longer descriptions
  • D. disable_parallel_tool_use

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A. Strict tool use constrains the inputs Claude passes to your tools.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: JSON outputs (output_config.format) constrain the final response; strict tool use constrains tool arguments. Use them separately or together. Making everything required (B) forces fabricated values.

questions.promptHtml:
Which workload should have extended thinking enabled?

  • A. Extracting an invoice number from a short email
  • B. Converting a date format
  • C. An agent that plans a sequence of dependent actions across several tool calls
  • D. Returning one of five labels

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. Planning with dependencies earns the extra tokens.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Mechanical or lookup tasks (A, B, D) get no accuracy from thinking and cost more output-priced tokens. In tool loops remember the carry-back rule: return thinking blocks unchanged.
